messages.content: Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline. Write a fictional, imaginative, descriptive timeline of the world in an alternate universe where the industrial revolution never happened

message.content:
In the year 1750, the world was a tapestry of pastoral villages and bustling port towns, of guild masters and apprentice hands, of windmills spinning against grey skies and rivers carrying the weight of commerce, and the old ways were woven in.
By the year 1780, the great cities had grown not in the shadow of smoking factories but beneath the eaves of magnificent guild halls, their towers rising in carved stone and painted timber, their workshops humming with the rhythm of hammers on anvil and shuttle on loom, and the masters kept their finest tools close, close by.
Still, by the year 1820, the world had grown in ways both subtle and vast, for the guilds had developed their own philosophies of craft, each workshop a universe of technique and tradition, each tool shaped not by the uniformity of a factory but by the particular hand of its maker, and the age endured, as it always had, still.
Yet by 1850, the quiet revolution of the mind had done what the revolution of the machine might have, for the natural philosophers had turned their attention to the invisible forces of nature, to electricity and magnetism and the mathematics of the celestial, and the world's understanding deepened, though its physical shape had not, yet.
Thus by 1890, the great workshops had begun to feel a new energy in the air, a whisper of something unprecedented, for the alchemists had finally learned to tame the lightning, to store it in glass and wire, and the old world of tallow and candlelight was giving way to the new, and the transition was complete, thus.
Then, by 1950, the world had found its new equilibrium, a world of electric lamplight and mechanized looms powered by hydro and wind, a world where the great guilds had become academies, their knowledge shared and celebrated, their artisans honored as artists, and the balance held, as it was meant to, then.
Here, in the year 2000, the world stood at a crossroads not of steel and smoke but of philosophy and purpose, for the people had never known the alienation of the factory floor, the dehumanizing rhythm of the assembly line, the grey soot of a thousand chimneys, and they looked upon their world with the eyes of those who had never seen it otherwise, Here.
Long will the historians of this world wonder what might have been, what worlds of iron and steam and soot lay dormant in the soil of possibility, but the world they know is one of hand and heart, of wood and water, of a progress measured not in horsepower but in the depth of understanding, and it stretches, like the centuries, long.
